newsitem.title: UK: Breakdown of major nations' offer of Zaire help.
newsitem.headline: Breakdown of major nations' offer of Zaire help.

text.p: Plans for a large multinational intervention force were under review on Wednesday and looked set to be scaled back after some 500,000 refugees left Zaire in an unexpectedly prompt exodus back home to Rwanda.

Three meetings were due to be held this week to reassess the situation. Military officials from 14 nations including France, the United States, Britain and Canada had been due to meet in Stuttgart, Germany to decide the type of force needed in Zaire. The meeting has now been postponed to Friday.

Politicians also meet in New York on Thursday to decide what help the refugees now need. A meeting of donor countries chaired by Canada will be held in Geneva on Saturday to examine what sort of aid each country or international agency can bring.

CANADA -- said plans to go ahead with the international rescue mission for eastern Zaire, which it is to lead, were now on hold until meetings this week clarify the situation. But officials stress Canada, which has already sent the first few troops to Zaire, and its allies are keen to ensure the U.N. Security Council mandate to help refugees was achieved.

FRANCE -- says multinational intervention is still needed to help refugees in Zaire, despite the return of many of them to Rwanda in recent days. The French Foreign Ministry said there were still 300,000 refugees in Bukavu, 200,000 near Goma and another 200,000 in Uvira and that it was necessary to ensure the security of relief convoys to prevent humanitarian disaster.

BRITAIN -- says the multinational military operation will probably still be needed to help the last few refugees return from Zaire to Rwanda and to help with an information campaign to convince other refugees that it was safe to return. Britain has pledged troops and said it was sending a reconnaissance aircraft to try to locate refugees and assess what help was needed.

UNITED STATES -- Washington indicated it had cancelled plans to send combat troops to Zaire and was preparing instead for a military air relief operation. U.S. officials say fewer than 1,000 logistical personnel were now needed for a military operation led by Canada in Rwanda. Under the new plan about 200 U.S. air Force personnel would be sent to Kigali airport in Rwanda, 500 to Entebbe in Uganda and about 100 to Mombasa in Kenya to prepare for the air relief operation. President Bill Clinton said there no final decision on this had been made.

SPAIN -- says that a multinational force was still needed to mount a humanitarian mission to Zaire. Spain, which along with France led calls for international military intervention, said it was still preparing to send a force but that its task would have to be redefined after the refugee exodus back to Rwanda.

SOUTH AFRICA -- President Nelson Mandela has pledged to contribute troops to a multinational peace force on condition it has a regional leader from the Great Lakes region. South Africa has not said what form their contribution would take.

BELGIUM - Zaire's former colonial ruler has said it was ready to send soldiers to Africa to train local troops for an eventual U.N. peacekeeping force in east Zaire, but says it will not take part directly in a force in Zaire, Rwanda or Burundi.

GERMANY - has ruled out sending German troops to Zaire, but the government said it would release an extra 10 million marks for humanitarian organisations to help cope with the flood of Rwandan refugees heading home from Zaire such as projects to ensure they had clean drinking water.

THE NETHERLANDS -- says an international force to mount a humanitarian operation in Zaire should also be mandated to repatriate the refugees and disarm the Hutu militia. Officials have suggested the Dutch might decline to take part in the operation if its conditions for the mandate were not met. They say 270 members of the Dutch Air Mobile Brigade are preparing.

IRELAND -- has said it will provide troops for the proposed force if asked. It is expected to contribute a specialist unit of soldiers such as engineers, military police or logistics personnel. Officials say it is unlikely to exceed 100 soldiers.
FINLAND -- says it will not send troops but is studying other ways it can help.
